paras: The reported lynching of Anthony Duffy and Bill Murphy refers to newspaper reports that two Black men who had testified for the State in the Laprade murder trial at Springfield, Tennessee, were hanged by a mob on the night of February 18–19, 1881. The reports followed the lynching of their five co-defendants from the Springfield court house that night and spread across the country as a one-line Nashville dispatch. Within days other dispatches said the two had not been caught and had escaped, so whether they were killed remains unsettled in the coverage.

Duffy and Murphy were among a group of Black men charged with the murder of L. S. Laprade, a farmer who lived alone near Sadlersville in Robertson County and was killed in September 1880. According to the papers, James Higgins named the others after a mob burned his feet, and two of the accused, Jack Bell and Archie Jamison, were taken from the Springfield jail and hanged that September. At the trial in February 1881 Duffy and Murphy turned State's evidence, and Duffy's testimony, printed by the Pulaski Citizen, placed Murphy at Laprade's gate on the night of the killing. The Kentucky Gazette's Springfield correspondent added that Duffy, fearing he would be hanged anyway, had earlier tried to kill himself in his cell.

The two were released on a nolle prosequi on Thursday, February 17, and went straight back to the neighborhood where Laprade had been killed. Several accounts held that their return provoked the mob, since people feared an appeal would leave the State without its witnesses.

On the night of Friday, February 18, a mob of about 200 armed men seized the five other defendants from the sheriff at the court-room door, just after the judge's charge, and hanged them from the court-house veranda. The Sun's Springfield dispatch said the lynchers "announced that they were going to pursue and lynch" the two released men, and the Cincinnati wire reported that "The mob are after them." According to the National Republican's correspondent, the mob split into three parties on leaving town, and one rode toward Laprade's house, near which Duffy and Murphy were known to be.

A Nashville dispatch of February 19 said it was "reported" that the two had been found hanging to a tree near Guthrie that morning. The New York World's Springfield dispatch, reprinted in Lancaster, stated it without qualification: both were found hanging "near the scene of the murder," making seven killed by the lynchers in one night. Other Springfield accounts reported only one death, with the National Republican saying Duffy's body was found on the road to Laprade's house and Murphy's hanging was only rumored, and specials to Memphis and Knoxville saying it was reported the mob had lynched Duffy during the night.

A coroner's jury held an inquest on the five men hanged at the court house and returned a verdict of death at the hands of persons unknown. No report of an inquest, identification or burial for Duffy or Murphy appears in the coverage. On February 19 the Tennessee Senate unanimously condemned the Springfield mob for taking prisoners from the custody of the court and called on the governor to bring the lynchers to justice. No arrests were reported, and the National Republican wrote that the lynchers remained "unknown and undisturbed."

The Nashville report traveled as a single sentence, headed "Two More of the Laprade Murderers Lynched" in the Richmond Dispatch and "The Other Two Served Likewise" in the Dallas Herald. Within two days it had run in papers from Savannah to Cheyenne, most of them keeping the qualifier "it is reported," and the Knoxville Chronicle's headline said the two were "Reported Lynched Also." Weekly papers repeated it for weeks: the Mower County Transcript in Minnesota placed Guthrie in Tennessee and called the hanging "The work of a vigilance committee," and the Pickens Sentinel in South Carolina stated it as fact on March 3.

The longer Springfield letters differed in tone. The World's dispatch said "Public sentiment sustains the action of the mob," while the Washington National Republican headlined "A Tennessee Mob's Vengeance" and called the killing of nine men "without warrant of law" a "sad comment upon the civilization of Tennessee." Nearly every paper called Duffy and Murphy "the Laprade murderers" although neither had been tried, and the Juniata Sentinel called Murphy "the last of the gang of black murderers."

Whether the two were killed is disputed. A Cincinnati dispatch of February 20 to the Commercial, printed by the Westminster Democratic Advocate under the heading "Duffy and Murphy Not Lynched," said they "were not caught by the lynchers in Robertson county." The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle, a Tennessee paper, wrote on February 26 that the two "made their escape, or else they would have shared the same fate." These denials came later than the February 19 reports, one of which called the hanging "A rumor not yet confirmed," but no account on either side names a witness, an inquest or an identified body.

The place is also uncertain: most wire copies said near Guthrie, Kentucky, one column said Guthrie, Tennessee, and the Springfield dispatches said near the scene of the murder or on the road to Laprade's house in Robertson County. Some wire copies also datelined the court-house lynching at Winchester, where a separate murder case was being heard that day, rather than Springfield.

reader.title: Reported lynching of Anthony Duffy and Bill Murphy
bases: Part of the mob that hanged five prisoners at Springfield was reported to have pursued and hanged Duffy and Murphy, two released co-defendants (A1, A9, A11); the killing itself is contested (A25, A26).

A mob of about 200 announced it would pursue and lynch the two men, who had been accused in the Laprade murder (A1, A2), and several papers reported them hanged (A9, A11), but the reports rest on rumor and were denied by a Cincinnati Commercial dispatch and a Tennessee paper saying they escaped (A25, A26, A28); the threat is documented, the killing is not established.

Many papers carried a Nashville 'it is reported' item and two Springfield dispatches said the bodies were found (A1, A9, A11), but a Feb. 20 dispatch said the two were 'not caught by the lynchers' and the Clarksville Chronicle said they escaped (A25, A26).

framing.detail: The Nashville rumor ran as a one-line item, headed 'TWO MORE OF THE LAPRADE MURDERERS LYNCHED' (Richmond) and 'THE OTHER TWO SERVED LIKEWISE' (Dallas), calling the two 'the Laprade murderers'.
The N.Y. World dispatch said 'Public sentiment sustains the action of the mob' and called the two 'murderers'.
The National Republican headlined 'A Tennessee Mob's Vengeance' and called the killings without warrant of law 'a sad comment upon the civilization of Tennessee'.
The Westminster Democratic Advocate printed the World account and then the correction headed 'DUFFY AND MURPHY NOT LYNCHED'.
